rationale: A wins because it knows where the story is strongest and where the floorboards are rotten. Its line, "Without the baseline, 22% is unpublishable," is exactly the kind of brake a founder needs before emailing reporters. B has good bones, but "Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" overstates the supplied fact, and "Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" imports a trend the update did not give it.
gaps_in_A: "studios get it whether or not they asked for it" is too assertive. Bundled pricing does not prove forced adoption or automatic rollout.
"That's a live change to how 50,000+ businesses run their schedules" overstates reach. Mindbody powers 50,000+ studios and salons; the update does not say all will use this assistant.
"waitlist backfill and no-show recovery are the two problems this reporter's readers complain about constantly" is plausible trade intuition, but it is not grounded in the supplied facts.
The take-private angle is honest about being thin, but "a recognizable PE playbook" still needs ownership and strategy evidence before it earns space as a kept angle.
gaps_in_B: "Rolling Out to 50,000 Studios" is the biggest offense. The update says Mindbody powers booking for over 50,000 studios and salons, not that the AI assistant is rolling out to all of them.
"While Fitness Apps Race to Build AI Coaches" manufactures an external trend and competitive frame not present in the update. That is not contrarian; that is borrowing scenery.
"Studio owner customer story — duplicate" is a bad refusal. A named pilot studio is a different protagonist from a data-methodology story and would likely be one of the most pitchable angles.

The next step says "journalist-fit-check" even though the set itself admits the 22% claim and ClassPass relationship need verification first. Match names after the load-bearing facts survive questioning.
